questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented for STI screening prior to having condomless sex. She had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus. She had a regular male partner and used barrier contraception with condoms. She had two lifetime sexual partners. Physical examination, including the pelvic exam, was unremarkable. Investigations: HIV 4th-generation Ag/Ab negative Rapid RPR reactive 1:4 Urine gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Send a blood sample for dark field microscopy
Treat for late latent syphilis with benzathine penicillin IM in 3 doses at 1 week intervals
Treat for primary syphilis with benzathine penicillin IM stat

questions.explanation: Perform a treponemal antibody test Falsely reactive RPR testing can occur in autoimmune diseases such as SLE. The RPR is based upon antigen synthesized from lecithin, cholesterol, and cardiolipin and reacts with antibodies produced in response to Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum infection. Similar antibodies can be formed in the setting of autoimmune diseases leading to a false-positive RPR. All reactive RPRs should be confirmed with a treponemal-specific test. Repeating an RPR will offer no diagnostic value. Dark field microscopy is not performed on blood samples but rather on specimens collected from chancres. In the absence of active lesions (primary or secondary syphilis) and with the concern for a false-positive result, therapy should be withheld until confirmatory results are available.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q24

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented to clinic with a “sore” on the shaft of his penis. He had noticed it 3 days earlier while showering. It was not painful. He denied dysuria or penile discharge. He returned from vacation in Panama 2 weeks ago. He reported unprotected sex with two female partners while in Panama. He had no known drug allergies. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed firm lesion, 1 cm in diameter on the shaft of his penis. Laboratory testing was obtained, including HIV fourthgeneration antibody test, urine gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT , and a syphilis EIA.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Administer benzathine penicillin IM for 3 doses at weekly intervals
Administer single dose of benzathine penicillin IM
Await syphilis screen and send a confirmatory antitreponemal test if positive
Refer to dermatology for further evaluation

questions.explanation: Administer single dose of benzathine penicillin IM Although appropriate testing should be performed, a patient with symptoms or signs of primary or secondary syphilis should be empirically treated at the time of presentation. Note also that syphilis serologic testing (either treponemal or nontreponemal tests) may not be immediately positive in primary syphilis. When suspicion is high, empirically treat (even when tests are negative). 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin is the treatment of choice for both primary and secondary syphilis. Evaluation of lesions for HSV-2 or HSV-1 is appropriate in this situation. However, the lesions are painless and empirical aciclovir is not indicated. Referral to dermatology could be considered if STI work-up and treatment did not result in recovery. (Image from Cox DJ, Ballard RC. Syphilis. In Morse SA, et al., eds. Atlas of Sexually Transmitted Diseases and AIDS. 4th ed. Saunders; 2010.)

He had been treated 24 hours earlier with 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin intramuscularly for a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. He reported four male sexual partners in the past 6 months, with inconsistent condom use. On exam, he was diaphoretic, his blood pressure was 96/56 mmHg, heart rate 106 beats/minute, and his temperature was 38.2°C. He had a diffuse macular rash which included the soles of his feet and his palms. There was no meningism. Investigations: Syphilis EIA positive RPR positive 1:128 Specific antitreponemal antibody positive HIV fourth-generation Ag/Ab test failed – please send a repeat
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Inflammatory response to dying spirochetes The patient has developed a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction after treatment of his syphilis. This syndrome is characterized by release of lipoproteins, cytokines, and immune complexes shortly after treatment. This reaction is characterized by fevers, chills, headaches, and myalgias. NSAIDs are recommended for treatment for these symptoms, and the reactions are usually self-limited.

questions.model_answer: (1) Previously treated syphilis - treponemal tests (CMIA, TPPA) remain reactive for life while the nontreponemal RPR reverts to negative. questions.model_answer: a) Three indications for LP: (1) Syphilis with neurologic, ophthalmic or otic signs/symptoms (regardless of stage). (2) Failure to achieve an adequate serologic response after therapy (no four-fold decline / serofast). (3) HIV-infected patient with serum RPR ≥1:32 or CD4 <350 cells/µL (higher risk of asymptomatic neurosyphilis — controversial). b) Two signs of treatment failure: (1) CSF pleocytosis fails to resolve (pleocytosis should clear within weeks to months). (2) Failure of CSF-VDRL to decline (or clinical progression / rising serum nontreponemal titre). c) Two key principles for HIV+ neurosyphilis with anaphylactic penicillin allergy: (1) Penicillin desensitization, then treat with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 MU/day IV — desensitization is preferred given penicillin's track record and limited ceftriaxone data. (2) If desensitization is not possible, use ceftriaxone 2 g IM/IV daily for 14 days, mindful of possible cross-reactivity in anaphylactic penicillin allergy.

cohort_answer.text:
Indications for LP (CID 2009): Presence of neurologic or ophthalmic symptoms or signs; Congenital syphilis; Previously treated patients who fail to achieve adequate serologic response to treatment; Tertiary syphilis (controversial, but in HIVinfo guidelines); HIV patients with neurologic symptoms/signs, late latent syphilis, RPR ≥1:32, CD4<350 cells/µL or treated syphilis with suboptimal decline in VDRL/RPR titre (some experts recommend CSF exam in all HIV-infected individuals); some experts recommend CSF exam in all patients with RPR ≥1:32.

B) Clinical progression; Increase in RPR/VDRL by ≥2 dilutions; CSF pleocytosis fails to resolve (should occur over 6 months, can take up to 2 years to normalize). CSF VDRL titre should decline 4x in 1 year but can take years to revert to negative; persistently high CSF-VDRL titre after tx may warrant retreatment. If CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein have resolved and serum VDRL has not risen, additional tx is unlikely beneficial.

C) Confirm penicillin allergy (history and allergist referral); desensitization to be attempted; consider alternative tx with Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h x14 days (or potentially Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x28 days, but not for neurosyphilis).

questions.question: The rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test.
questions.question_raw:
Q84 (2006 AM)
RPR test

parts.text: Explain how it works.

parts_raw.text: A) Explain how it works?

questions.model_answer: a) The RPR is a nontreponemal (antilipoidal antibody) test. It measures the ability of the patient's serum to flocculate/agglutinate a standardized suspension of cardiolipin, cholesterol, and lecithin antigen. In the RPR card test, finely divided charcoal particles are incorporated as a macroscopic visualizing agent, so flocculation is read by eye (unlike the VDRL, which is read microscopically). Titre roughly correlates with disease activity, making it useful for monitoring treatment response.

cohort_answer.text: Rapid plasma reagin: looks at ability of heat-inactivated serum to flocculate or agglutinate suspension of cardiolipin cholesterol lecithin antigen. Finely divided charcoal particles used for visualization (Mandell's)

questions.question: A mother is diagnosed with syphilis and her baby is asymptomatic at birth. For each of the following maternal-treatment scenarios, state how you would manage the neonate.
questions.question_raw: Congenital syphilis. Baby asymptomatic.

parts.text: Mother treated at 37 weeks with a single dose of IM penicillin.
Mother treated early with IM penicillin x 3 doses; maternal RPR fell from 1:64 to 1:2; baby's RPR is 1:2.
Mother treated early with maternal RPR falling from 1:32 to 1:2; baby's RPR is undetectable.

parts_raw.text: A) Mom treated at 37 weeks IM pen x 1
B) Mom treated early with IM penicillin x 3. RPR 1:64 dropped to 1:2. Baby RPR 1:2
C) Mom treated early 1:32 to 1:2. Baby undetectable

questions.model_answer: a) Treatment completed <4 weeks before delivery is considered inadequate, so the infant is classified as probable congenital syphilis regardless of the normal exam. Perform full evaluation (quantitative non-treponemal test, CBC/platelets, CSF for VDRL/cell count/protein, long-bone radiographs, and audiology/ophthalmology/LFTs as indicated) and treat with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IV q12h for the first 7 days then q8h to complete 10 days (or procaine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM daily x 10 days). b) Mother adequately treated early with an appropriate (>4-fold) decline in titre, and baby's RPR (1:2) is not 4-fold higher than the mother's: congenital infection is unlikely. Baseline exam plus serologic follow-up; a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM may be given if follow-up is uncertain. c) Mother adequately treated early with >4-fold titre decline and baby non-reactive: lowest risk. Clinical and serologic follow-up alone, with non-treponemal titres expected to be non-reactive by 6 months; treat only if titres rise or the infant becomes symptomatic.
questions.beyond_mandell: The scenario-specific neonatal evaluation and the 4-fold titre/4-week treatment thresholds and serologic follow-up schedule are from the CDC/AAP congenital syphilis algorithm; Mandell supplies the 'inadequately treated' definition and the CS penicillin regimen.

cohort_answer.text:
Because mom was treated within 4 weeks of delivery, considered inadequate. Requires full work up: syphilis serology, LP with cell count/VDRL/protein (as clinically indicated: long bones x-ray, audiology, ophtho). Treat baby with Pen G 50,000U/kg IV q12h x first 7d then q8h for total 10 days
Since mom was treated before 4 weeks from delivery, and baby is asymptomatic, unlikely congenital syphilis. Presumably late latent treatment; baseline and monthly exams for 3 months with serology @0,3,6,18 months. No further assessment unless becomes symptomatic or RPR higher than mom's or does not resolve. RPR should trend down by 3 months, nonreactive at 6 months. Treponemal tests negative by 12-18 months
Over 4-fold decrease in titer and treated early. If no risk of reinfection and titer remains low and baby titer not 4-fold above mom's, do baseline with monthly exams for 3 months and serology @0,3,6,18 months

questions.question_raw: Congenital syphilis

parts.text: How do you make the diagnosis?
What is the treatment?

parts_raw.text: How do you make the diagnosis?
Treatment?
C) List 4 clinical situations where you would want to specifically look for congenital syphilis?

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis rests on a combination of maternal, clinical and laboratory criteria: an infant born to a mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis at delivery; a reactive infant treponemal test; direct detection of T. pallidum (darkfield microscopy, PCR, or silver/immunohistochemical staining) from lesion exudate, placenta, umbilical cord, or nasal discharge; plus supporting findings - clinical signs (hepatosplenomegaly, rash, jaundice, anemia), long-bone radiographic changes, abnormal CSF cell count/protein, reactive CSF VDRL, or a reactive IgM test. b) Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IV q12h for the first 7 days of life then q8h for a total of 10 days, or procaine penicillin G 50,000 U/kg IM daily for a minimum of 10 days. c) (1) Mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis at delivery; (2) Mother treated with a non-penicillin regimen; (3) Inadequate maternal serologic response (<4-fold decline in titre) or treatment not documented; (4) Syphilitic stillbirth (fetal death after 20 weeks with untreated/inadequately treated mother) or clinical signs of syphilis in the infant.
questions.beyond_mandell: The 'treated within 4 weeks of delivery' criterion and abnormal placenta/cord prompt are from CDC guidance; Mandell grounds the other situations (inadequate/absent maternal treatment, non-penicillin therapy, stillbirth >20 weeks, infant signs).

Maternal: Primary/secondary/early latent - benzathine penicillin G 2.4mU IM x1 dose. Late latent - benzathine pen G 2.4mU IM weekly x3 weeks. Infant: Crystalline penG IV 50,000U/kg q12h x first 7d then q8h for total 10 days

questions.model_answer: a) Early primary infection: non-treponemal (RPR) tests lack sensitivity early and are non-reactive in roughly 30% of early primary cases, whereas treponemal tests become reactive 1-2 weeks after the chancre and remain reactive for life; the rising RPR (now 1:16) reflects evolving/under-treated infection or reinfection. b) Evaluate the infant: quantitative RPR/VDRL compared to the mother (should be <4-fold of maternal titre) and full physical exam; if the infant titre is 4-fold greater than the mother's or the exam is abnormal, treat as proven/highly probable congenital syphilis with penicillin G x 10 days; if reinfection is suspected, full workup with empiric treatment. c) (1) Reactive CSF VDRL; (2) CSF pleocytosis and/or elevated protein; (3) Long-bone radiographic changes (metaphyseal lucency/periostitis); (4) Thrombocytopenia or anemia. d) Vertical transmission is highest with untreated primary/secondary (early) maternal syphilis, approaching 60-100%, with substantial risk of stillbirth and perinatal death; risk falls with later maternal stage. e) A positive treponemal test in the infant most likely reflects passively transferred maternal IgG; repeat the treponemal test at 15-18 months (should become non-reactive if uninfected) and repeat the RPR at ~3 months to exclude incubating congenital syphilis - treat if either remains/becomes reactive.
questions.beyond_mandell: Stage-specific vertical-transmission percentages, the specific radiographic signs (e.g. Wimberger sign, metaphyseal osteochondritis), and the timed infant serologic follow-up (persistence of maternal treponemal antibody to ~15-18 months) derive from CDC/epidemiologic data; Mandell grounds the serologic explanation, CS criteria and treatment.

cohort_answer.text:
Early primary infection - non-treponemal tests become positive 4-6 weeks after infection while treponemal tests become positive earlier and once positive most remain positive despite tx. OR reinfection (consider especially if high risk)
Test baby for RPR/VDRL to ensure titer is 4x less and not greater than mom; infant physical exam. If abnormal to either, baby has proven or highly probable congenital syphilis and treat with PenG x10 days IV. If mom high risk (possible reinfection), full workup with empiric treatment
Lab: CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose); VDRL+ in CSF; Thrombocytopenia; anemia. Radiographic: Symmetrical long bone lesions; Metaphyseal osteochondritis; Wimberger's sign; Diaphyseal periostitis; Osteitis (celery stick appearance); Dactylitis
Vertical transmission depends on maternal stage: Primary/Secondary untreated 70-100% (25% stillbirth, 14% neonatal death, 41% congenital infection, 20% healthy). Early latent 40%. Late latent 10%
Treponemal antibody may remain positive up to 15 months postnatally (maternal Abs), repeat at 18 months should be negative. Repeat RPR at 3 months to rule out incubating congenital syphilis. If positive at all for both, baby warrants tx for congenital syphilis

questions.model_answer: a) Contact within 90 days of a person with early syphilis warrants presumptive (epidemiologic) treatment even if seronegative: send syphilis serology (treponemal screen plus RPR) and give benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose; repeat serology to confirm. b) Treat with stage-appropriate penicillin as for a non-pregnant patient - benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM for early syphilis; because she is in the third trimester some clinicians give a second dose one week later, and penicillin is the only satisfactory agent in pregnancy. Repeat RPR and follow, and evaluate the neonate at birth. c) There is no acceptable non-penicillin alternative in pregnancy (tetracyclines are fetotoxic, macrolides risk failure, ceftriaxone data are insufficient), so she must be desensitized to penicillin and then treated with benzathine penicillin G. d) Treated at 28 weeks is >4 weeks before delivery and, if adequate and with an appropriate serologic response, is considered adequate treatment: examine the infant for signs of congenital syphilis, obtain a quantitative RPR compared to the mother (should be <4-fold), and follow clinically and serologically; treat with IV penicillin G x 10 days if the exam is abnormal or the infant titre is 4-fold above the mother's.
questions.beyond_mandell: The neonatal evaluation/follow-up thresholds (4-fold titre, 4-week adequacy rule) are CDC/AAP guidance; Mandell grounds presumptive contact treatment, stage-based regimens and mandatory desensitization in pregnancy.

cohort_answer.text: Not pregnant/no allergies: Syphilis screen (CMIA for serology, then RPR and TPPA); Rx benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM x1; repeat RPR at 6 months; treat all sexual contacts in past 90 days with 1 dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4mU IM x1. Pregnant at 36 weeks: Syphilis screen and RPR; Rx benzathine pen G 2.4MU IM (1 or 3 doses depending on stage); repeat RPR at 6 months; examine baby (CBC/platelets, CSF cell count/protein/quantitative VDRL, other tests as indicated e.g. CXR, long-bone films, eye exam, LFTs, neuroimaging, ABR). Anaphylaxis to PCN: desensitize to penicillin and give benzathine pen G 2.4MU IM weekly x1-2 doses; repeat RPR at 6 months; examine baby and repeat mom's RPR and do serum/CSF VDRL of baby. Some experts recommend two doses of benzathine penicillin G-LA 2.4 million units one week apart particularly in the third trimester (difficulty staging, pregnancy PK changes, possible benefit). Baby follow-up: examine for abnormalities of congenital syphilis; clinical evaluation at 2,4,6,12 months; repeat RPR at 2-3 months until negative (should decrease by 3 months, negative by 6 months); if baby RPR 4x or more than mom's, proven/highly probable congenital syphilis, treat with 10 days IV pen G; a reactive RPR at 18 months is diagnostic of congenital syphilis (maternal treponemal antibodies can persist until 15 months).

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis; Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1, L2, L3) - lymphogranuloma venereum, first line rx is doxy x21 days; Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis/granuloma inguinale): first line is azithro +/- gent, but doxy or Septra x3 wks are alternative regimens

questions.question: Syphilitic aortitis is suspected in a patient with positive CMIA, TPPA, and FTA-Abs but a negative RPR.
questions.question_raw:
Q81 (2013 PM)
Syphilis aortitis suspected with + CMIA, TPPA, FTA-Abs and negative RPR

parts.text: Explain the serologies in the context of aortitis.

parts_raw.text: A) Explain the serologies in the context of aortitis

questions.model_answer: a) Aortitis is cardiovascular (late/tertiary) syphilis. Treponemal tests (CMIA, TPPA, FTA-ABS) are highly sensitive and, once reactive, remain reactive for life, so they stay positive in late disease. Nontreponemal tests (RPR) are less sensitive in late syphilis and approximately one-third of tertiary patients have a nonreactive nontreponemal test, presumed to reflect a burned-out inflammatory response; RPR can thus become nonreactive over time. A reactive treponemal test is sufficient evidence to treat, and these patients still require stage-specific therapy despite the negative RPR.

cohort_answer.text: Tertiary syphilis. Test sensitivity with nontreponemal tests is lower (71-73%) while high for treponemal specific tests (94-96%). In late syphilis, nontreponemal tests could become nonreactive over time

questions.model_answer: a) Early syphilis, non-primary non-secondary (early latent): asymptomatic with documented seroconversion within the previous 12 months. b) Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose; this is the recommended regimen for early syphilis regardless of HIV status. c) Doxycycline 100 mg PO bid for 14 days (or tetracycline 500 mg PO qid for 14 days); ceftriaxone 1-2 g IM/IV daily for 10-14 days is an alternative - azithromycin is not recommended in this setting.

cohort_answer.text: Stage: Early latent - asymptomatic with a negative test within 1 year (if no negative test within last year, automatically late latent). Treatment: 1x dose benzathine penicillin 2.4M units, given as 2x1.2M unit doses IM to each buttock. Alternatives: Doxy 100mg PO BID 10-14 days, ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM daily 10-14 days
